extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether prior acts (use, experiments, exhibitions, or lost arts) defeat novelty / priority of a patent — i.e., when an earlier disclosure amounts to a completed reduction to practice vs. a mere experiment or lost/abandoned art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice / completed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea or structure must be reduced to a practical, useful form — a completed invention — before it can be treated as prior invention that defeats a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What kind of use is necessary depends on the character of the invention; mere conception is insufficient. Until actual use has ascertained the capacity of the structure to effect what is proposed, there is no completed invention. Example: Conner's safe required testing (e.g., exposure to fire) to show it worked as the theory proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior experiment will not invalidate later invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior experiment or experimental trials do not invalidate a subsequent completed invention unless the prior work was brought to a practical, completed form capable of producing some useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior machines must be working machines, not mere experiments; they must have actually done work or been capable of doing it. Duration of use is immaterial except insofar as it shows experiment vs. completion. (Citations: Agawam Co. v. Jordan; Seymour v. Osborne; Whitely v. Swayne.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure alone may in some cases show completed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain cases a perfect or complete structure, by its construction alone, may be sufficient to infer a completed invention even absent actual use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where complete invention can be inferred from the structure alone, evidence of a machine being 'perfect' and taken away to be used may be sufficient to invalidate a later patent without proof of prior actual use. (Example: Parker v. Ferguson; water-wheel case.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings or representations are insufficient to defeat a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere representation of an idea by drawings does not constitute embodiment into practical and useful form that will defeat a granted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person must have reduced the idea to practice and embodied it in some useful practical form; drawings alone do not satisfy this requirement. (Citations: Poppenhusen v. N.Y. Gutta-Percha Comb Co.; Ellithorpe v. Robinson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability to perform (operative capacity) can substitute for actual public use
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that a prior machine have been actually used for its contemplated purpose if it was capable of such use and its adaptation to such use was within the knowledge of a mechanic of competent skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A completed, perfected piece of mechanism capable of working successfully may defeat novelty even if not actually used before the later invention; exhibition and explanation to skilled persons may impart such knowledge. (Coffin v. Ogden.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption in practical use is strong evidence of reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting an invention into practical use is generally strong evidence that it was reduced to practice (i.e., a completed invention rather than an experiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But use is not strictly required for most inventions to show completion; adaptation and capability may suffice. If use is merely experimental, the invention is not perfected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use vs secret/experimental use — material distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: To set aside a patent on the ground of prior 'public use', the prior practice must be more than mere experiments; it must be in public use and operation among persons in the trade likely to know it, not merely secret or confined experimental use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English authorities distinguish 'public use' as use in a public manner (not merely by the public generally). Under U.S. law, publicity of prior use is relevant only as circumstantial evidence whether there was a completed invention. Jury inquiries focus on whether prior uses were experimental or complete and public (Cornish v. Keene; Jones v. Pearce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment / discontinuance is significant when assessing whether prior use was perfected
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a prior inventor abandoned or discontinued the use is material evidence on whether the prior practice was only experimental and unsuccessful or was a perfected invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior practice was abandoned because it failed or was forgotten, it may not bar a later patent; but if there was a prior perfect invention, abandonment before the later patent date is immaterial. Jury must weigh abandonment as circumstance to determine completeness (Househill Co. v. Neilson; cited House of Lords guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost art / reinvention may permit patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A rediscovery of a previously existing but long-forgotten or 'lost' art can, under some circumstances, be treated as a new discovery eligible for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish two classes: (a) where an existing article discloses its mode of construction (possession proves knowledge of method), and (b) where the method of manufacture cannot be proved by the article alone and knowledge of the process is lost. In the latter, recovering the process may be a new discovery. (Illustrations and dicta from Neilson and Gaylor v. Wilder.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether prior machine was substantially the same despite inferiority
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior machine may be inferior or perform less well than a later machine, but if it is substantially the same and was a perfected invention it anticipates the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferiority in performance does not prevent a prior perfected machine from anticipating a later patent so long as the two accomplish substantially the same result. (Cases: Woodman v. Stropson; Swift v. Whisen; Rich v. Lippincott.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony on hypothetical operability has limited relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a prior machine 'would have worked' or 'would have operated' is relevant only insofar as it tends to the inference that the thing actually did work; this tendency is often slight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts being asked whether an alleged prior device would have worked bears on the ultimate factual inference of whether the prior thing actually operated as a completed invention, but such testimony is indirect and of limited weight.
